And every one of those mornings started the same way, a wooden kitchen chair,
a small silver radio and a five-minute radio Taiso warm-up we did together.
Her name was Fumiko. She lived in a small town
north of Sendai, in a wooden house with a narrow garden and a screen door that
stuck in the summer. She lived to 98 and she walked every one of those
days. When she was 90, she could still walk to the fish shop and back without
stopping. People in the town knew her walk.
Small steps, one hand on her hip, one hand with the shopping bag.
She never ran, she never hurried, she just went. I taught physical education for
32 years, boys and girls, middle school, on a schoolyard with
more dust than grass. I taught them volleyball, running, jump rope,
and I taught them to stretch before the bell. And after I retired, I taught
the neighbour women in their 70s how to do these same movements while sitting on a chair.
They came to my living room on Tuesdays, some of them in their slippers. So,
them, done on a chair, five minutes, and at the end I'll tell you what to look for
after two weeks. You don't need a gym, you don't need a mat, a kitchen chair
the seat, feet flat, as wide as your hips,
Back straight, like a string pulls the top of your head. Good. One small test before we
start. It takes 10 seconds and I do it every morning.
Stand up from your chair once, slowly, without using your hands,
and sit down again. That is it. Don't hurry it,
don't be brave, and don't judge it. Just notice how it feels.

Five movements. Number one, arms up.
Number two, shoulder rolls. Number three, seated marching.
Number four, ankle circles. Number five, deep
breathing with a slow arm lift. That is the whole routine my grandmother did
for 60 years. Nothing fancy. Nothing expensive.
One chair, one radio, five minutes. Let's begin
ten times. Both arms rise slowly up to the ceiling and
at the same time the heels lift from the floor. Only the heels.
The toes stay down. Then arms down, heels down. Ten times.
Slow, like the string on your head is pulling up, and your hands just follow it. Why
does arms up matter? Because of the balance. When you reach up, the body
finds where it is. The shoulders open and the chest opens with it. And
the heels? The heels teach the ankles they still have a job. Standing balance
in a chair. My grandmother did this one first, always
to count with me in Japanese. Ichi, ni, san.
She never once missed ten. Ten times, count out loud with me.
One, two, three, slowly, four, five,

The shoulders are where I keep my mornings. When I was teaching, I carried a bag of exams in one
hand every day for years, and my right shoulder sat up by my ear by Friday.
I would rub it in the staff room, and the history teacher would say, Kurosawa
you will notice. Your hands go down. When the shoulders loosen, the hands
hang beside the chair instead of climbing up to the ears.
Stand in front of a mirror if you have one. That is the whole test. Where are my hands?
Why it matters. The neck, the tops of the shoulders, the inside of the
shoulder blades. That is where the stiffness lives after a night in bed. Ten circles
and they open a little. The first day may be one centimetre.
The two months may be more. Ten back. Count with me.

Movement number three. Seated marching. Back straight, hands on the seat of the chair
or on your knees if that is easier. Now pick up one foot,
set it down, pick up the other, set it down. Like a marching soldier
knee a little, not high. Little is fine. Why marching in a chair?
Because it wakes the hip. The hip is a big joint and it likes to
be used. When you lift the knee, the front of the hip opens and the thigh
does the work and the circulation. The blood moves down to the feet
waiting for the rice to finish cooking. She said, march while the rice
cooks and the rice will not wait for you. She marched 20 steps in
the kitchen beside the pot. 20 steps, count out loud. 1,
18, 19, 20. Good. Movement number 4.
Ankle circles. Sit up straight. Lift one foot just
a little off the floor. Now draw a circle with the toes.
Like you are drawing a circle on a table with a pencil, and the pencil is your big toe.
Ten circles one way, ten circles the other way.
Then the other foot. Same, gentle, never fast.
Why the ankle? Because the ankle is the door to the ground.
Every step you take starts at the ankle. If it is stiff, the walk
is short and careful. Little circles open that door again.

On the bad days, I did them with her. One foot each,
sitting side by side on that chair. Then the other foot. Ten circles.
Breathe slowly while you draw. And when you finish, rest
the foot on the floor and shake it gently like shaking water off your hand.
Movement number 5. Deep breathing with a slow arm lift. Sitting
and lift the arms out to the sides and up to the ceiling. At the top,
hold for one slow breath. Then lower the arms as you breathe out, five times,
only five, and each one slower than the last.
Why breathing? Because the body is not only the legs.
When we breathe slowly, the whole body slows down with us. And a slow breath before you
stand up makes the standing easier. It is like a small pause before the music.
My grandmother finished this way every morning for 60 years.
Arms up, breathe in, arms down, breathe out.
Then she would say, now the day can start. And she stood up and she went out.

If you forget everything I said today, keep two words,
slow and together. Slow is strong because a slow movement lets
the body answer you. Together is kind because you do not
have to do all five on the first morning. One is enough,
one movement ten times in your nightgown before the tea.
